trial_name: FAST — Screening Frequency and Spontaneous Breathing Trial Techniques (2024)
citation: Burns KEA, Wong J, Rizvi L, Lafreniere-Roula M, Thorpe KE, Devlin JW, et al. Screening Frequency and Spontaneous Breathing Trial Techniques: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024;332(21):1808-1821
one_liner: In adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, protocolised more-frequent-than-once-daily screening did not accelerate liberation; when combined with pressure-supported SBTs it unexpectedly prolonged time to successful extubation (HR 0.70).

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years US, ≥16 years Canada) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation >24 h with FiO₂ ≤0.70 and PEEP ≤12 cm H₂O, able to trigger breaths
pico.intervention: More frequent screening (≥twice daily) and/or pressure-supported SBT with PEEP (PS >0 to ≤8 cm H₂O, PEEP >0 to ≤5 cm H₂O, duration 30–120 minutes)
pico.comparison: Once-daily screening and/or T-piece SBT (unsupported breathing)
pico.outcome: Time to successful extubation (sustained unsupported breathing for ≥48 hours)

background.existing_knowledge: Liberation from mechanical ventilation can occupy a large proportion of ventilator time and delays increase ventilator-associated complications and resource use. Routine practice includes readiness screening followed by spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs). Two widely used SBT approaches differ in loading: low-level pressure-supported SBTs (often with PEEP) vs unsupported T-piece trials. Clinical trials before FAST yielded mixed signals; practice variation persisted. Guideline panels permit several SBT approaches and prioritise protocolised liberation, but left uncertainty about whether increased screening frequency accelerates successful extubation.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty whether protocolised more frequent screening (vs once-daily) and/or pressure-supported SBT with PEEP (vs T-piece) shortens time to successful extubation, and whether the two interventions interact.
background.hypothesis: More frequent screening and/or pressure-supported SBT with PEEP would reduce time to successful extubation. The factorial design assumed no mechanistic reason for interaction between screening frequency and SBT technique.

methods.design: Multicentre, pragmatic, open-label, 2×2 factorial RCT with central randomisation stratified by centre using variable block sizes. Enrolment was weekday daytime only to align with protocolised screening workflows.
methods.setting: 23 ICUs in North America (US and Canada)
methods.intervention: Screening frequency: at least twice daily (06:00–08:00 and 13:00–15:00), with additional screening at clinician discretion; missed screens completed within 6 h. SBT technique: pressure-supported SBT with PEEP — PS >0 to ≤8 cm H₂O, PEEP >0 to ≤5 cm H₂O, duration 30–120 minutes.
methods.comparison: Screening frequency: once-daily (06:00–08:00). SBT technique: T-piece unsupported breathing; during COVID-19 positivity, T-piece could be performed while connected to a ventilator circuit without inspiratory support (protocol amendment).
methods.blinding: Open-label; clinicians and bedside staff unblinded, extubation decisions clinician-driven within protocolised structure.
methods.sample_size_power: 760 patients required to detect a 1-day median reduction in time to successful extubation (from 5.0 to 4.0 days) with 80% power at 5% two-sided significance, assuming no interaction.
methods.primary_outcome: Time to successful extubation (sustained unsupported breathing for ≥48 h).
secondary_outcomes: 6-month functional outcomes (EuroQol-5D, Functional Independence Measure) in consenting survivors
methods.follow_up: In-hospital through day 60; 90-day mortality; 6-month patient-centred outcomes in alive, consenting patients.

headline_bullets: Main effects non-significant: screening frequency HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.76–1.03, P=0.12); SBT technique HR 1.06 (95% CI 0.91–1.23, P=0.45).
Significant interaction for primary endpoint (P=0.009) required pairwise contrasts.
More frequent screening + pressure‑supported SBT prolonged time to successful extubation versus once‑daily + pressure‑supported (median 3.9 vs 2.0 days; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50–0.96, P=0.02).
No significant differences in mortality or major complications; adverse events related to screening or SBT were uncommon.

safety: Adverse events related to screening/RSBI: 2/198 (1.0%), 2/204 (1.0%), 4/195 (2.0%), 3/200 (1.5%) across the four factorial groups.
Adverse events related to SBT conduct: 0/198 (0%), 5/204 (2.5%), 3/195 (1.5%), 1/200 (0.5%).

domains.notes: Central randomisation stratified by centre, variable block sizes; allocation concealment robust. Factorial design assumed no interaction, which was later violated, reducing efficiency.
Open-label; clinicians unblinded, extubation decisions clinician-driven — plausible pathway for behaviour-mediated effects and interaction.
Modified ITT: 837 randomised, 797 analysed. 28 patients excluded after randomisation, 12 withdrawn due to lack of data permission; debated as potential bias.

Substantial separation in screening dose: mean screenings per patient-day 3.9 and 4.8 in once-daily arms vs 7.9 and 7.6 in more frequent arms; SBTs per patient-day 1.9 and 2.1 vs 3.3 and 2.6. Major screening violations 4.6–6.6%, major SBT violations 3.8–10.2% across groups.
Groups well balanced: mean age 61–64 years; ~59% male; median SOFA 5–6; predominant indication acute respiratory failure (~55–62%).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong: randomisation and protocol separation are solid, but lack of blinding, clinician-driven extubation, and post-randomisation exclusions/withdrawals introduce plausible bias — especially relevant given the unexpected interaction.

domains.notes: Broad adult medical/surgical ICU case-mix with moderate severity; applicable to typical invasively ventilated adults beyond the first 24 h. Exclusions (profound neurological impairment, tracheostomy, prolonged ventilation >2 weeks) limit inference for neurocritical care and chronic weaning populations.

North American staffing models (respiratory therapist availability) may influence feasibility and effect of more frequent screening. Variable PS/PEEP ranges and SBT duration increase pragmatic relevance but reduce mechanistic precision. Few COVID-19 patients, so subgroup certainty is limited.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate for adult medical/surgical ICUs with comparable staffing and weaning infrastructure; limited for neurocritical care, prolonged weaning cohorts, and settings where screening frequency is constrained by workforce.

strengths: Large, multicentre, pragmatic factorial design addressing two common, protocolisable weaning strategies.
Clinically meaningful primary outcome (sustained unsupported breathing ≥48 h) rather than surrogate SBT pass.
Prospectively published protocol and statistical analysis plan (including COVID‑era update).
limitations: Open‑label implementation with clinician‑driven extubation decisions (risk of behaviour‑mediated effects).
Modified intention‑to‑treat with post‑randomisation exclusions/withdrawals (28 excluded, 12 withdrawn; debated).
Within‑arm variability in PS/PEEP and SBT duration (PS 0–8 cm H₂O, PEEP 0–5 cm H₂O; 30–120 min).
6‑month outcomes available only in consenting survivors, increasing attrition bias risk for long‑term endpoints.

critical_appraisal.summary: FAST is a well-designed factorial trial that yielded a surprising interaction: more frequent screening combined with pressure-supported SBTs paradoxically prolonged time to extubation, challenging the common assumption that more screening is better. The open-label design and modified ITT raise concerns, but the finding is consistent with clinician-behaviour interactions and warrants replication.
strengths: Prospectively registered and powered factorial design
Pragmatic, multicentre conduct enhancing external validity
weaknesses: Lack of blinding and clinician-driven extubation introduce potential bias
Unexpected interaction not supported by prior mechanistic reasoning

sections.authors_conclusion: Protocolised ‘more frequent’ screening should not be assumed to accelerate liberation, particularly in systems using pressure-supported SBTs with PEEP; in FAST, this combination prolonged time to successful extubation and increased ventilation hours/ICU stay. Once-daily screening remains a defensible default when combined with structured SBTs.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not adopt protocolised more-frequent-than-once-daily screening as a standalone quality metric; if using pressure-supported SBTs with PEEP, increased screening may paradoxically delay extubation. Once-daily screening with structured SBTs is a safe default pending replication.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult medical/surgical ICU patients without prolonged ventilation or tracheostomy, in settings with similar staffing models.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That more frequent screening is inherently harmful in all contexts; the interaction was observed with pressure-supported SBTs only, and T‑piece outcomes were similar regardless of frequency.
implementation_caveats: Monitor SBT technique and clinician decision thresholds if increasing screening frequency.
Replicate the finding before changing protocolised weaning bundles.

controversies.notes: Not mechanistically anticipated; editorial commentary emphasised the interaction may reflect complex clinician behaviour and workflow effects, not a biological effect. Structured credibility assessment (ICEMAN) underscores that unexpected interactions require replication and plausible mechanism before practice change.
28 patients excluded after randomisation, 12 withdrawn due to lack of permission to use data. Published correspondence challenged the risk of bias; authors defended the modified ITT analytic set.

Systematic reviews/meta-analyses post-FAST suggest pressure-supported SBTs may increase extubation success without higher reintubation, but effect sizes are modest and context‑dependent. Network meta-analyses rank several techniques but highlight uncertainty from heterogeneity and indirectness.

Recent practice guidance continues to endorse protocolised liberation and permits multiple SBT techniques, emphasising careful selection, monitoring, and avoidance of unnecessary prolongation of ventilation.

unresolved_questions: Is the interaction real or an artefact of unblinded, behaviour-mediated effects?
Would replication confirm harm or simply null effect of more frequent screening with pressure‑supported SBTs?
How do different staffing models and rigidly standardised SBT protocols modify the interaction?
Are long‑term functional outcomes different (data limited by attrition)?

numbers_to_remember: Primary: screening HR 0.88 (0.76–1.03), SBT HR 1.06 (0.91–1.23), interaction P=0.009
More frequent + PS: time to extubation HR 0.70 (median 3.9 vs 2.0 d)
No mortality difference, adverse events rare
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Protocolised more-frequent-than-once-daily screening with pressure-supported SBTs may paradoxically delay extubation; once-daily screening remains the safer default.
